meta.title: AI Bubble Tracker
meta.thesis: The AI capex/circular-financing structure fails not when the numbers fall — it fails when they stop accelerating. Watch the speed, not the level.
meta.crisisFrame: 2006: loans failed when prices rose 8% instead of 15%. Watch the speed.

verdict.compositeNote: A quieter week on the surface — no fresh funding round, no backlog earnings (Oracle's next report isn't until Sept 9-12), and no kill-trigger event — but the picture underneath still leans toward acceleration, with two new cracks worth watching. Nvidia's Aug 26 earnings (record $96.2B revenue, Data Center alone at $89B) reiterated hyperscaler capex climbing toward $1.3T next year from about $800B now — the spending story keeps getting bigger, not smaller. But the market's patience for that spending is thinning: Meta fell about 10% after a JPMorgan downgrade tied to raising its own capex guidance to $125-145B without matching revenue proof, the second time in two weeks (after Alphabet) that a capex RAISE has been punished rather than a capex cut being rewarded — still not the kill trigger, but the same underlying nervousness. On the Treasury side, a weak 20-year bond auction in mid-August briefly spiked long yields and set off a sharp same-day selloff in AI-adjacent stocks (CoreWeave -8.3%, Tempus AI -6.9%) before the government's doubled bond buybacks calmed things down — a live example of the 'fear transmits into AI stocks through Treasury stress' mechanism this tracker watches for. Then, on Aug 28, incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to suggest interest-rate hikes might still be needed given elevated inflation — a hawkish surprise that pushed short-term yields back up and complicates the idea that the government's bond buybacks alone can keep borrowing costs pinned down. Revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic and the funding-round ladder are essentially unchanged from last week (still no public IPO filing or pricing for either), and Chinese AI models continue to gain usage share (readings cluster 51-61% of OpenRouter traffic, still noisy) even as DeepSeek's newest model bucked the 'nearly free' trend with a 14x price increase.

stack.requirement: Leases stay current + structures keep finding buyers

stepUpLadder.name: The Step-Up Ladder
stepUpLadder.question: Does OpenAI's next raise price above the last, and by how much?

nextExpected.note: Smallest step-up ever — at the exact moment free Chinese models attack the growth that justifies it — S-1 confidentially filed 2026-05-22; window Q4 2026–early 2027 (see IPO Watch)

notes.text: The step-up multiple IS the collateral. Like 2006 house prices, the ladder doesn't need to fall to break the structure — it just needs to stop climbing at the required rate.
notes.attribution: Jay Martin, The Jay Martin Show

notes.text: No new round this week. OpenAI completed a $7B employee tender offer (~Aug 10) priced at its existing $852B valuation — confirms the last round's value but isn't a new step-up data point since no new investor priced it higher. Anthropic's own employee tender reportedly fell short of the roughly $6B investors wanted to buy; treat that report cautiously since the valuation reference attached to it looks stale. Neither company has filed a public S-1 or set a price range yet.

backlog.name: The Backlog
backlog.question: Do the backlogs keep GROWING, or do they just stay large? Not the same thing.

concentration.note: ~50% owed by OpenAI + Anthropic — neither profitable. >50% of Oracle's backlog traces to OpenAI alone. Research-firm estimates (via Eisman, Aug 2026): ~70% of hyperscaler AI revenue and 25–35% of total cloud revenue comes from Anthropic + OpenAI.

backlog.trigger: Backlog growth rate declines two consecutive quarters = decelerating; flat/shrinking = broken
backlog.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); platform earnings backlogs (RPO)

notes.text: The dependency of the hyperscalers on Anthropic and OpenAI is just huge — both lose billions and rely on raising capital for survival. Oracle's debt is rated barely above junk. There is no hedge for the LLMs: hyperscalers have fallback franchises, the labs don't.
notes.attribution: Steve Eisman, The Real Eisman Playbook

notes.text: First full read across all four hyperscalers: Microsoft's commercial backlog jumped to $678B (from $625B), closing in on Oracle's $638B. Google Cloud posted $155B (+82% YoY) and Amazon's AWS posted ~$200B — both reported here for the first time. Backlog growth is not just an Oracle story anymore; it's broad-based across the sector.

No fresh backlog figures this week — Microsoft, Google and Amazon already reported their quarters, and Oracle's next earnings (fiscal Q1 FY27) isn't until Sept 9-12, which is this signal's next real checkpoint.

capex.name: Capex Acceleration
capex.question: The day the market rewards a company for LEAVING the race is the day the race is over.
capex.keyFact: 2026: first year construction spend exceeds combined operating cash flow of the four platforms — every marginal dollar is debt-funded, borrowed against backlog owed by unprofitable borrowers

killTrigger.description: A tech giant announces it is cutting AI data-center spending — and its share price goes UP on the news
killTrigger.explainer: Right now investors treat every extra billion of AI spending as good news, so cutting back would normally hurt a stock. The day the market cheers a company for spending less, investors have stopped believing the race is worth winning. That is the clearest early sign the boom is turning — it would show up long before any crash.

capex.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); hyperscaler capex guidance

notes.text: Nvidia's $500B securitized-financing push means some data-center capex shifts off hyperscaler cash flow — hyperscaler FCF 'could improve' optically while the debt stack extends into banks and private credit. Read improving FCF with suspicion from here.
notes.attribution: Steve Eisman, The Real Eisman Playbook

notes.text: Kill-trigger watch candidate: Meta is getting squeezed — latest quarter revenue +28% but expenses +55%, no cloud business to monetize AI through. Most likely first major player to cut; watch how the market reacts when it does.
notes.attribution: Steve Eisman, The Real Eisman Playbook

notes.text: The five biggest spenders (Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle) now guide to a combined $775-800B for 2026 — roughly 3x the ~$238B spent in 2024. This is the opposite of the kill trigger so far: Alphabet RAISED its 2026 capex guidance (to $195-205B) and its stock fell about 7% over the following week — a capex increase punished, not a capex cut rewarded. That's still consistent with the current framing (investors want the spending to keep climbing), just a reminder the market is getting twitchier about how big the numbers are getting.

Still no kill trigger, and the numbers keep climbing: Nvidia's Aug 26 earnings (record $96.2B quarterly revenue, Data Center alone $89B, Q3 guided to $108B) had its CFO reiterate that the top hyperscalers' combined capex is heading toward roughly $1.3T next year, up from about $800B now. But the same 'raise-without-proof gets punished' pattern repeated: Meta fell about 10% on a JPMorgan downgrade after guiding 2026 capex up to $125-145B, the second capex raise in three weeks (after Alphabet) to get sold off rather than bought. Microsoft and Amazon, whose capex raises are tied to demonstrated cloud revenue growth, are not seeing the same reaction — the market is starting to price the difference between spending that's paying for itself and spending that isn't.

chinaShare.name: China Share Pressure
chinaShare.question: Chinese models don't need to be better. Nearly as good and nearly free is enough.

events.text: Moonshot releases Kimi K3 — #1 on coding leaderboard within a day, beating Anthropic and OpenAI blind at ~40% lower cost
Kimi K3 open-sourced — free to download and self-host

chinaShare.mechanism: Pulls customers away AND forces down prices American labs can charge — both push on the speed of US AI revenue growth. The speed is the collateral.

history.label: US model share of OpenRouter usage (%)
US model share of OpenRouter usage (%)

chinaShare.source: OpenRouter usage share via The Jay Martin Show (Aug 2026)

notes.text: Red here does not mean Chinese models are failing — it means pressure against US share is RISING. This signal measures the force pushing on US revenue speed.

Independent corroboration: enterprises are using Chinese open-weight models more and more; 'overcharging for tokens is going to be very difficult with good-enough competition.' A price war is possible — and Anthropic + OpenAI are ~70% of hyperscaler AI revenue, so a price war transmits straight into the backlog.
notes.attribution: Steve Eisman, The Real Eisman Playbook

notes.text: New Chinese releases kept coming this week (Alibaba's Qwen3.8 Max Aug 2, Z.AI's GLM-5.2 Turbo Aug 17), but the readings on actual Chinese-model traffic share are noisy right now — trackers show anywhere from ~45% to over 60% of OpenRouter volume depending on whether you measure the top 10 models or all traffic. Treat the exact percentage as uncertain this week; the direction (more competitive Chinese releases, more enterprises adopting them) is not.

More Chinese releases (Z.AI's GLM-5.3-Flash Aug 26) and readings still cluster high, 51-61% of OpenRouter traffic by some trackers, with DeepSeek the single largest provider at roughly 16%. One genuine crack in the 'nearly free' narrative: DeepSeek's new V4 Pro model raised prices roughly 14x with new peak/off-peak billing — the first sign a leading Chinese lab thinks it can charge more, not less. Moonshot's Kimi K3 reportedly had to pause new subscriptions due to demand. Keep treating the precise percentage as noisy; the competitive pressure itself is not in question.

revenueSpeed.name: Revenue Speed
revenueSpeed.question: Is US AI revenue growth still accelerating?

openai.lossNote: Loses tens of billions/yr; has never earned a profit

history.label: OpenAI annualized revenue run-rate ($B) — doubled since spring 2026

revenueSpeed.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); TechCrunch/CNBC/Axios reporting on Anthropic + OpenAI run-rates, Aug 17 2026

notes.text: Both labs are still accelerating, not just growing. Anthropic told investors its annualized revenue run-rate hit $65B in July — up 7x from a year earlier — and investors expect it to keep growing at roughly that pace, finishing 2026 around $100-120B. OpenAI's run-rate reached about $40B, roughly double where it stood in the spring. This is the strongest reading this signal has had — moved from 'watch' to 'accelerating' this week — but both companies are still deeply unprofitable, so the speed is what's propping up their valuations, not earnings.

No fresh run-rate print this week — largely a restatement with texture: Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue came in above $11.5B versus $787M a year earlier, and OpenAI's enterprise revenue passed its consumer revenue for the first time in July, with its paying customer count up 32% in a single month. Nothing here suggests deceleration; there's just no brand-new number to move the needle beyond what was already captured last week.

policyWatch.name: Policy Watch
policyWatch.question: Ban or no ban — either path stresses the structure.
policyWatch.headline: No Adversarial AI Act introduced in both House (H.R.4142) and Senate (S.2177), referred to committee — debate has become bill text
policyWatch.interpretation: The catfish effect run backwards — China used competition to grow strong; a US ban removes the pressure that forces improvement while cutting US businesses off from a nearly-free tool. Either path stresses the structure: ban → protected stagnation; no ban → growth curve flattens. This week the debate moved from talk to an actual bill (restricting federal agencies and contractors from using AI from 'foreign adversarial' entities), though it hasn't been voted out of committee yet and enforcement is questionable since open-weight Chinese model files are already freely downloadable.
policyWatch.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); Washington policy debate coverage; Congress.gov H.R.4142 / S.2177

notes.text: No movement this week — H.R.4142 / S.2177 remain in committee with no markup or floor vote found, and no other new Chinese-AI restriction bill or executive action surfaced. Ladder holds at DRAFT_LEGISLATION.

concentration.name: Index Concentration
concentration.question: Know what you actually own.
concentration.note: An index fund is not 500 businesses — nearly half is one bet on one belief: that America owns the future of technology.
concentration.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); S&P index weights

notes.text: Reconfirmed this week at the same ~40-41% level — no material change. Still record-high concentration, just not moving faster or slower than before.

Eased to about 37.6% as of Aug 28, down from ~40-41%. Still within the range this measure has bounced around in recent months and still historically extreme concentration — not read as a material de-concentration of the index.

treasuryStack.name: The Treasury Stack
treasuryStack.question: In the next crisis, the fear points AT the belief that funds the Treasury.
treasuryStack.interestVsDefense: Interest now exceeds the entire military budget
treasuryStack.watch: Auction bid-to-cover + 10Y behavior during AI-led selloffs: in 2008 scared money BOUGHT treasuries (fear pointed at banks). An AI crash points fear at the belief in American growth itself — scared money may walk.

history.label: 2-year Treasury yield (%) after Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, up from 4.22%

treasuryStack.source: The Jay Martin Show — 'The 2006 Question' (Aug 2026); US Treasury data; Aug 13 2026 30-year bond auction results

notes.text: First concrete auction data point for this signal: the Aug 13 30-year bond auction ($31.3B) drew a bid-to-cover of 2.39 — weaker than the trailing 12-month average of 2.43 — at a high yield of 5.216%, the highest 30-year yield in 25 years. Demand wasn't a failure, but it was softer than normal at a moment when the government needs buyers to keep showing up. Worth watching whether this is noise or the start of a trend.

The exact mechanism this signal watches for showed up live: a weak 20-year Treasury auction in mid-August briefly pushed 30-year yields above 5.08% and triggered a sharp same-day selloff in AI-adjacent stocks (CoreWeave -8.3%, Tempus AI -6.9%) before the Treasury's doubled bond buybacks calmed the market back down. Then, on Aug 28, incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to say rate hikes may still be needed given elevated inflation — a hawkish surprise that pushed 2-year yields from 4.22% to 4.30% and complicates the idea that buybacks alone can keep the government's own borrowing costs pinned down. Two genuinely new threads for this signal, both pointing the same direction: rising long-term borrowing costs are now visibly colliding with AI-linked asset prices.

securitization.name: Compute Securitization Watch
securitization.question: When compute becomes securitized collateral, who ends up holding the paper — and does the remittance data start publishing?

deal.structure: Nvidia partnering with six large asset managers on a $500B financing push treating AI data centers like commercial real estate or toll roads — structure unclear, securitizations assumed
deal.shift: Until now AI data centers were financed by hyperscaler cash flow and corporate debt. This moves some financing into securitized paper held by banks and private credit.

securitization.interpretation: The most literal 2006 rhyme yet: debt collateralized by payments owed largely by two unprofitable borrowers (OpenAI and Anthropic), relocating off hyperscaler balance sheets into banks and private credit. Watch for a masking effect — hyperscaler free cash flow can LOOK better while the risk relocates rather than shrinks.
securitization.metaNote: Eisman shorted subprime because Moody's securitization database published monthly delinquency data. He says no such dataset exists for AI. If these deals securitize, monthly remittance data on compute-lease payments would eventually become exactly that dataset — the first real credit tape for the AI buildout.
watchItems: Deal structure disclosure — true securitization or just secured lending?
Who holds the paper: banks, private credit, insurers?
Whether monthly remittance/delinquency data starts publishing
Hyperscaler FCF optically improving while consolidated leverage rises
securitization.source: The Real Eisman Playbook — weekly rap, week ending Aug 14, 2026 (recorded Aug 13); Nvidia Newsroom Aug 11 2026; SEC guidance coverage

notes.text: The deal now has names attached: Nvidia formalized memorandums of understanding with six of the biggest names in finance — Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR — to raise the $500B+ in compute financing. Two new details sharpen the risk picture: the SEC issued guidance in July that removes a risk-retention rule which would otherwise have required sponsors to keep a slice of this debt on their own books, and Nvidia has personally guaranteed (with its own money) that the chips used as collateral will hold their value. Both moves make it easier for capital to flow into these deals and easier for the risk to end up somewhere other than where it was created — exactly the 2006 dynamic this signal is watching for.

Still MOUs, not signed final agreements, and still no remittance or delinquency data publishing. But the SEC guidance behind the deal (dated Aug 17 in wider coverage) got more scrutiny this week: it explicitly takes sponsors 'off the hook' on certain look-through requirements for data-center securitizations. BlackRock's Larry Fink compared the moment to the birth of the mortgage-backed-securities market in the 1970s — which, read straight, is either a compliment about unlocking capital or an omen, depending on how this decade's version ends.

ipoWatch.name: IPO Watch
ipoWatch.question: Where do Anthropic and OpenAI price vs their last private rounds — and how do they trade after? Weak aftermarket = this thesis accelerates.

companies.name: Anthropic
companies.expectedWindowNote: Consensus among underwriters, media, and prediction markets points to an October 2026 Nasdaq listing — roughly 6 weeks out as of Aug 17
companies.valuationNote: Reports split between ~$1T (barely above the $965B last private round — a ~1.0x step-up, the weakest ever) and $2T+ (investor expectations — would be the largest IPO in history). The spread IS the tell: where it actually prices is the step-up data point.

companies.name: OpenAI
companies.expectedWindowNote: Targeting a debut 'as soon as Q4 2026', but reporting this week (Digitimes, Aug 20) says OpenAI has told employees a listing could wait until 2027 — an earlier date remains possible if conditions improve, but the company itself is now hedging the timeline. No ticker, price range, or confirmed date yet
companies.valuationNote: Groundwork laid for a listing at up to $1T — an implied 1.17x step-up from the March 2026 $852B round, the smallest ever (see The Step-Up Ladder)

ipoWatch.postIpoFields: Populated by the weekly sweep once each company lists: offerValuationB, firstDayClosePctVsOffer, day30PctVsOffer, currentPctVsOffer

thresholds.intact: Prices within/above target range AND holds above offer for 30+ days
thresholds.warning: Prices below the low end of expectations, or trades below offer within 30 days
thresholds.broken: Prices below last private round (a public down round), or breaks the offer price and stays below — thesis accelerates

ipoWatch.interpretation: The IPOs are where the step-up ladder finally meets a real market. Eisman: 'When OpenAI and Anthropic go public, we will have some real data. Until then, we have supposition.' Pricing below the last private round is the public-market version of the 2006 moment, and weak aftermarket trading transmits straight into hyperscaler revenue credibility — these two companies are ~70% of hyperscaler AI revenue.
